title: A prime-editing-based strategy for pooled protein tagging and subcellular localization mapping - Nature Cell Biology
byline: Sanchez; Henry M; Mani; Deepak C; Lapidot; Tomer; Serebrenik; Yevgeniy V; Shalem; Ophir
html:
Abstract

The subcellular organization of proteins carries important information on cell state and gene function, yet there are limited technologies that enable routine measurements of protein localization at scale. Here we develop pooled endogenous protein tagging using prime editing to image subcellular localizations for many proteins in parallel within a heterogeneous cell pool. We constructed three prime editing libraries comprising 17,280 prime editing guide RNAs (pegRNAs) to exhaustively tag 60 endogenous proteins spanning diverse localization patterns and explore a broad space of genomic and pegRNA design parameters. We integrate pegRNA features into a predictive computational model for tagging efficiency to constrain the search space of effective pegRNAs for large-scale peptide knock-in. Last, we show that combining in situ pegRNA sequencing with deep learning image analysis enables scalable exploration of subcellular organization, setting the stage for systematic studies of proteome dynamics across cell types and perturbations.

Main

Systems-level understanding of cellular state and gene function requires technologies for visualizing proteins in their endogenous regulatory context at scale. Endogenous gene tagging enables the installation of generic molecular handles with high specificity to target and visualize any protein expressed in living cells. Arrayed generation of endogenously tagged cell lines coupled with deep learning image analysis has provided unique insights into cellular organization and protein function1. Yet, as such approaches still rely on the delivery of gene-specific reagents (for example, homology-directed repair (HDR) templates) in an arrayed format, they remain labour intensive and limited in scale. Adapting gene tagging to a pooled format will enable unprecedented insight into changes in proteome organization in response to genetic and environmental perturbations.

As endogenous tagging through HDR requires the delivery of both a targeting sequence and a donor insertion template, the lack of tools for paired delivery has limited the development of HDR-based pooled tagging. A way to avoid the need for gene-specific donors is to use a generic donor and rely on non-homologous end joining. Such a strategy has been used for pooled tagging at the carboxy (C) terminus, which has a limited choice of single guide RNAs, resulting in low success rates and unpredictable edits in the coding region2,3. To combine generic donors with large insertion site flexibility, we have previously developed intron tagging4. This approach has been used to isolate a large array of endogenously tagged cell clones5,6. We have expanded this approach to directly target proteins for misfolding7 and to search for proteins with degradation function through induced proximity8, demonstrating the utility of pooled endogenous gene tagging for biological discovery. However, as approaches mediated by non-homologous end joining (1) require separate delivery of DNA donors, (2) insert tags in random orientation and unrestricted copy number, (3) require multiple libraries to tag three coding frames and (4) rely on double-strand breaks, which frequently induce indel mutations and carry the risk of genomic rearrangements, there remains a technology gap to advance pooled tagging as a standard functional proteomics modality.

The development of prime editing has introduced a versatile method for genome editing that facilitates precise targeted insertion9,10. Prime editing uses a DNA nickase fused to a reverse transcriptase that is guided to a target site of interest by a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) encoding the desired edit in its 3′ extension. Although it is limited in insertion size, this approach has many advantages for pooled tagging as it: (1) enables the scarless insertion of peptides in both amino (N) and C termini without generating double-strand breaks; (2) uses a single reagent capable of encoding target recognition and editing in an RNA template; (3) has minimal off-target editing; and (4) works across diverse cell types.

Prime editing has been used successfully for pooled genome editing aimed at modelling prime editing efficiency11,12,13,14 and high-throughput investigation of variant effects15,16, yet its application to pooled insertions at multiple sequence-distinct loci across the genome has been limited—probably due to generally low insertion efficiencies associated with single-flap prime editing, as well as a lack of feature-sufficient pegRNA design models for larger insertions. Here we focused on developing a scalable and modular approach for pooled N and C terminus tagging using prime editing and a split fluorescent protein system17,18. We show that low multiplicity of infection (MOI) lentiviral delivery of pegRNAs is compatible with efficient gene tagging. We next develop a two-step cloning strategy for the construction of large-scale pooled pegRNA libraries to exhaustively tag 60 endogenous proteins covering diverse localization patterns, while exploring a wide range of pegRNA parameters across distinct, native genomic loci for their association with knock-in efficiency. Our analysis revealed both genomic and pegRNA features influencing tagging efficiency, which we integrated into a predictive model for pegRNA-mediated gene tagging. Finally, integrating pooled prime tagging with in situ pegRNA sequencing and automated widefield microscopy allowed us to resolve localizations of individual tagged proteins directly within pooled libraries. The single-cell images provide rich training data for machine learning models that capture the full spectrum of localization patterns, together forming a scalable pipeline for exploring subcellular proteome organization under diverse cellular contexts and perturbations. Custom prime tagging libraries can be designed at www.primetagging.org.

Results

Low-MOI pegRNA transduction enables efficient protein tagging over time

In practice, adapting genome editing tools to a high-throughput pooled format requires obtaining robust editing efficiency following lentiviral delivery of guides at low MOI. To test this, we first designed a piggybac vector for delivery of the prime editor (PE2) with both antibiotic- and fluorescence-based selection, to be used together with the mNG3K(1–10) component of a split fluorescence protein system17,18 (Fig. 1a). We then engineered cell lines stably expressing both components. First, cells were transfected with the prime editor piggybac donor and transposase, followed by blasticidin selection. Selected cells were then transduced at high MOI with lentiviral particles containing mNG3K(1–10) and transfected with an exogenous CLTA gene fused to the NG(11) peptide tag to transiently make mNG3K(1–10)-expressing cells recoverable by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). We then sorted clonal cell lines for the expression of both components using a near-infrared fluorescent protein (emiRFP670; ref. 19) and green fluorescence as expression indicators for PE2 and mNG3K(1–10), respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

a, Vector design for the piggybac prime editor and lentiviral split mNG3K(1–10) reporter (157993; Addgene). b, Workflow for prime-editing-mediated endogenous protein tagging in an engineered prime editing and split mNeonGreen reporter HEK293T line. c, Top, tagging efficiency over time for two engineered clonal lines expressing PE2 at different expression levels and lentiviral delivery of an NG(11) peptide insertion encoding pegRNA targeting the C terminus of H2BC21 at different MOIs. The data represent means ± s.d. from n = 3 individual pegRNA transductions for each timepoint and condition. Bottom, emiRFP670 fluorescence distributions by flow cytometry for the two engineered clonal lines with respect to wild-type HEK293T cells. emiRFP670 is expressed in tandem with PE2 using a self-cleaving P2A peptide sequence; emiRFP670 fluorescence serves as a proxy for prime editor expression. d, Flow cytometry dot plot at day 28 after transduction of a pegRNA targeting the C terminus of H2BC21 for NG(11) tagging. e, ×60 confocal image of NG(11)-tagged H2BC21 in post-sort HEK293Ts. Scale bar, 20 μm. f, Sanger sequencing trace for an NG(11)-tagged H2BC21 allele with intended PAM disruption compared to areference allele with the expected NG(11) insertion edit, obtained from sorted tagged cells following one pegRNA transduction. Source numerical data are available. Panel b created in BioRender; Sanchez, H. https://biorender.com/4ci8r8s (2026). CAG, cytomegalovirus enhancer/chicken β-actin promoter/rabbit β-globin splice acceptor; hPGK, human phosphoglycerate kinase 1 promoter; ITR, inverted terminal repeat; LTR, long terminal repeat; mU6, mouse U6 small nuclear RNA promoter; PAM, protospacer-adjacent motif; RTT, reverse transcription template; SFFV, spleen focus-forming virus promoter; UTR, untranslated region.

After establishing stable cell lines with both components, tagging endogenous proteins can follow from the delivery of pegRNAs encoding the NG(11) peptide targeted to either the N or C terminus of a protein of interest, followed by self-complementation with the stably expressed mNG3K(1–10) (Fig. 1b). To test the efficiency of tagging, we produced lentiviral particles containing a pegRNA designed to tag H2BC21 at the C terminus and transduced at different MOIs. We tested two clonal lines, with high and low PE2 expression, and measured the tagging efficiency using flow cytometry at weekly timepoints (Fig. 1c,d). In both clones, we observed an increase in efficiency over time with the PE2 high-expressing clone achieving more than 10% at day 28. We validated tag insertion precision by both microscopy of sorted polyclonal cells (Fig. 1e) and sequencing of the target site (Fig. 1f). Thus, using clonal lines selected for high PE2 and mNG3K(1–10) expression, we were able to achieve high efficiency tagging with low-MOI pegRNA delivery, providing the basis for endogenous protein tagging in a pooled format.

Design and construction of large-scale pooled pegRNA libraries for exploring design parameters associated with tagging efficiency

We next set out to build pooled pegRNA libraries to explore the effects of genomic and pegRNA features on tagging efficiency across many genes. We selected 60 genes with diverse localization patterns1, validated N or C terminus tagging sites (30 genes for each terminus) and at least one spacer-programmed nick in each 15-base pair (bp) bin of a −30 to +30 bp target window flanking the insertion site (Fig. 2a). Four spacers were selected for each gene and spacers with the highest specificities20 were prioritized within each targeted 15-bp bin. For each spacer, we designed 72 pegRNAs exploring various parameters, including primer binding site (PBS) length, distance between the nick and insertion point, tag insertion size and reverse transcription template (RTT) homology length distal to the nick site (Fig. 2b). Each pegRNA was designed with a twin containing synonymous codon mutations in the tag insertion template to serve as internal pegRNA replicates (termed opti and anti). A resulting parent library of 17,280 pegRNAs was divided equally into three libraries (5,760 pegRNAs) corresponding to three NG(11) tag insertion sizes of 48, 60 and 78 bp. The three independent libraries covered the same pegRNA design parameter space with the exception of tag insertion length and linker sequences, allowing us to assess the consistency of the contribution of each pegRNA feature to tagging efficiency. We included 240 non-targeting control pegRNAs in each library for a total of 6,000 pegRNAs in each. We added a unique 12-bp barcode downstream of the pegRNA 3′ extension for the identification of each library member by bulk amplicon sequencing and in situ barcode sequencing. To construct the pooled pegRNA plasmid libraries, we developed a two-step cloning strategy in which the spacer and 3′ extension are separated by two type-IIS restriction sites and synthesized together in 300-nucleotide oligos. In the first step, oligo pools containing these pegRNA intermediates are amplified and cloned into a CROPseq vector we modified to accept pegRNA libraries while retaining compatibility with single-cell and in situ sequencing approaches. In the second step, the constant pegRNA scaffold is inserted through another large-scale cloning reaction (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1b and Methods).

a, Selection of 60 genes covering diverse subcellular localizations annotated by OpenCell. Each gene’s terminus targeted for tagging and nicking locations for prime-editing-mediated tag insertion is shown. b, Combinations of pegRNA design parameters explored across the parent library, which was split into three libraries by tag insertion length: 48, 60 or 78 bp. Each library was cloned separately in two consecutive large-scale cloning steps, starting with a pegRNA oligo pool. c, Schematic of the generation of a pooled tagged cell library. d, Flow cytometry dot plot at day 23 after transduction of the 60-bp tag pegRNA library before sorting tagged library cells. e, ×40 widefield fluorescence imaging of the sorted 60-bp tagged cell library showing diverse localization patterns, suggesting that a different protein is tagged in each cell. Two representative fields from one pooled imaging experiment are shown (scale bar, 50 μm) with boxed regions enlarged in the centre (scale bar, 20 μm). f, Spacer barcode recombination rates at different stages of library construction. g, Violin plots showing targeting and non-targeting control distributions of pegRNA log2[fold change] (log2[FC]) values for each double-sorted tagged cell library relative to presort day 23. For the inner box plots, the white dots represent median values, the box edges represent interquartile ranges (25th to 75th percentiles) and the whiskers extend to values within 1.5× the interquartile range. Sample sizes for targeting and non-targeting controls, respectively, were: n = 5,427 and 240 for the 48-bp library; 5,424 and 240 for the 60-bp library; and 5,444 and 239 for the 78-bp library. As expected, most pegRNAs were depleted in sorted cell populations, with a long tail of enriched pegRNAs observed primarily in the targeting group. h, pegRNA spacers ranked by Benjamini–Hochberg FDR-corrected q values from one-sided Kolomogorov–Smirnov tests comparing the log2[fold change] distribution of pegRNAs for each targeting spacer with the log2[fold change] distribution of non-targeting pegRNA controls within each library. At an FDR of 10%, 108, 105 and 163 of 240 spacers were considered active in the 48-, 60- and 78-bp libraries, respectively. At the gene level, 41, 48 and 56 of 60 genes had at least one active spacer in the 48-, 60- and 78-bp libraries, respectively. All genes had at least one active pegRNA spacer across the three libraries. Source numerical data are available. sgRNA, single guide RNA.
